lead: BPSK carries one bit in the phase of a carrier. The transmitter sends cos(2πf<sub>c</sub>t) for a 1 and its negative for a 0, so the two signals are exact opposites. This antipodal pair gives the smallest binary error probability in white Gaussian noise. BPSK appears in GPS navigation, deep-space links and low-rate control channels where power matters more than bandwidth.
prereq: You need Unit 5 on matched filters, signal space and AWGN error analysis, plus 6.1 for binary passband signals.

blocks.text: BPSK sends one bit per symbol. For bit 1 the transmitter sends a carrier with phase 0; for bit 0 it sends the same carrier with phase π. The two waveforms are negatives of each other.

blocks.where: E<sub>b</sub> is the bit energy in joules, T<sub>b</sub> is the bit duration in seconds, f<sub>c</sub> is the carrier frequency in hertz, and the plus sign sends bit 1 while the minus sign sends bit 0.

blocks.text: The amplitude √(2E<sub>b</sub>/T<sub>b</sub>) is not arbitrary. Squaring s(t) and integrating over one bit gives E<sub>b</sub>. The factor 2 cancels the average of cos² over a whole number of cycles.

items: Convert the input bits to bipolar NRZ: bit 1 becomes +1, bit 0 becomes −1.
Multiply this bipolar waveform by the carrier A cos(2πf<sub>c</sub>t), where A = √(2E<sub>b</sub>/T<sub>b</sub>).
The product is the BPSK signal. A data change from +1 to −1 flips the carrier phase by 180°.

blocks.text: The multiplier is a balanced modulator. The output has constant envelope, so a nonlinear power amplifier can be used. Some syllabi call BPSK phase reversal keying (PRK).
The receiver must know the carrier phase. It multiplies the received signal by a local carrier and integrates over one bit.

blocks.where: r(t) is the received signal plus noise, y is the test statistic in volts, E<sub>b</sub> is the bit energy, and n is the noise component after integration.

blocks.text: The integrator output is compared with a threshold at zero. If y > 0 the receiver decides bit 1; if y < 0 it decides bit 0. The local carrier must be phase-locked to the incoming carrier. A squaring loop or a Costas loop can recover it.

On a signal-space diagram BPSK has two points on one axis: +√E<sub>b</sub> for bit 1 and −√E<sub>b</sub> for bit 0. The distance between the points is 2√E<sub>b</sub>. The decision boundary is the line through zero, so each point owns a half-plane.

A phase error θ in the local carrier multiplies the useful signal by cos θ. The error probability rises because the effective bit energy falls to Eb cos²θ. 6.3 treats the case where the phase is unknown.
In AWGN the bit error probability is set by the distance between the two constellation points.

blocks.where: P<sub>b</sub> is the bit error probability (dimensionless), E<sub>b</sub> is the received bit energy in joules, N<sub>0</sub> is the one-sided noise power spectral density in watts per hertz, Q is the Gaussian tail probability, and erfc is the complementary error function.

blocks.text: The Q function is Q(x) = (1/√(2π)) ∫<sub>x</sub><sup>∞</sup> e<sup>−u²/2</sup> du. The complementary error function is erfc(x) = (2/√π) ∫<sub>x</sub><sup>∞</sup> e<sup>−u²</sup> du. They are related by Q(x) = ½ erfc(x/√2).

With rectangular pulses the BPSK spectrum is a sinc-shaped band around f<sub>c</sub>. The null-to-null bandwidth is 2R<sub>b</sub>, where R<sub>b</sub> is the bit rate in bits per second. The spectral efficiency is R<sub>b</sub>/(2R<sub>b</sub>) = 0.5 bit per second per hertz.

Coherent orthogonal BFSK has P<sub>b</sub> = Q(√(E<sub>b</sub>/N<sub>0</sub>)). To reach the same P<sub>b</sub> as BPSK, BFSK needs twice the E<sub>b</sub>/N<sub>0</sub>. That is a 3 dB energy advantage for BPSK. The price is that BPSK needs carrier phase recovery.

figure.caption: Bipolar data multiplies the carrier; the receiver multiplies by a local carrier, integrates over one bit and slices at zero. The threshold is the only decision device.

spec.title: BPSK transmitter and coherent receiver
spec.aria: Bipolar data multiplies a carrier, crosses a channel, multiplies a local carrier, integrates, and passes a zero threshold to output bits.

examples.question: A BPSK link sends data at R<sub>b</sub> = 1 Mbps. The received E<sub>b</sub>/N<sub>0</sub> is 10 dB. (a) Find the bit error probability. (b) Find the expected number of bit errors in 10<sup>8</sup> transmitted bits.
examples.answer: The bit error probability is about 3.87×10<sup>−6</sup>, so about 387 bit errors are expected in 10<sup>8</sup> bits.
examples.check:
import math
ebno_db = 10.0
ebno = 10**(ebno_db/10)
x = math.sqrt(2*ebno)
pb = 0.5*math.erfc(x/math.sqrt(2))
errors = 1e8*pb
print(f"{pb:.2e}")
print(f"{errors:.0f}")

traps: Forgetting the factor 2: BPSK uses Q(√(2E<sub>b</sub>/N<sub>0</sub>)), not Q(√(E<sub>b</sub>/N<sub>0</sub>)). The second form belongs to coherent orthogonal BFSK.
Using symbol energy E<sub>s</sub> in place of bit energy E<sub>b</sub>. For BPSK one symbol carries one bit, so E<sub>s</sub> = E<sub>b</sub>. Confusing them with QPSK gives wrong numbers.
Saying BPSK and QPSK have different bit error probability for the same E<sub>b</sub>. With Gray coding they have the same P<sub>b</sub>; their symbol error probabilities differ.
Taking the null-to-null bandwidth as R<sub>b</sub>. For rectangular BPSK it is 2R<sub>b</sub>, so the spectral efficiency is 0.5 bps/Hz.
Ignoring carrier phase. BPSK detection is coherent; a phase error θ reduces the effective E<sub>b</sub> by cos²θ.

quiz.q: What do the plus sign and the minus sign mean in the BPSK waveform s(t) = ±√(2E<sub>b</sub>/T<sub>b</sub>) cos(2πf<sub>c</sub>t)?
quiz.a: Plus sends bit 1; minus sends bit 0. The two waveforms differ by 180° in phase.
The two signal vectors are equal in length and opposite in direction: +√E<sub>b</sub> and −√E<sub>b</sub>. Their inner product is −E<sub>b</sub>, not zero.

quiz.q: A BPSK system has E<sub>b</sub>/N<sub>0</sub> = 7 dB. Find P<sub>b</sub>.
BPSK and coherent orthogonal BFSK must both give P<sub>b</sub> = 10<sup>−5</sup>. Which needs less E<sub>b</sub>/N<sub>0</sub> and by how much?
quiz.a: BPSK. Q(√(2E<sub>b</sub>/N<sub>0</sub>)) = 10<sup>−5</sup> gives E<sub>b</sub>/N<sub>0</sub> ≈ 9.6 dB. BFSK needs Q(√(E<sub>b</sub>/N<sub>0</sub>)) = 10<sup>−5</sup>, so E<sub>b</sub>/N<sub>0</sub> ≈ 12.6 dB. BPSK saves about 3 dB.

quiz.q: A BPSK link sends R<sub>b</sub> = 2 Mbps with rectangular pulses. Find the null-to-null bandwidth and the spectral efficiency.
quiz.a: B = 2R<sub>b</sub> = 4 MHz. Efficiency = 2 Mbps / 4 MHz = 0.5 bps/Hz.

quiz.q: Write Q(x) in terms of erfc(x).
The local carrier has a phase error of 30°. By what factor does the effective E<sub>b</sub> fall, and what is the loss in dB?
quiz.a: Effective E<sub>b</sub> becomes E<sub>b</sub> cos²30° = 0.75E<sub>b</sub>. Loss = −10 log₁₀(0.75) ≈ 1.25 dB.

quiz.q: State the two constellation points of BPSK and the decision boundary.
quiz.a: Points at +√E<sub>b</sub> and −√E<sub>b</sub> on one axis. Decision boundary is the zero line, y = 0.

beyond: Not for the exam. BPSK is the reference modulation in GPS, deep-space telemetry, and many RFID and power-line links. Practical receivers use Costas loops or decision-directed phase tracking. Search 'BPSK bit error rate', 'Costas loop', and 'antipodal signalling' for hardware detail. Modern systems often move to QPSK or QAM when bandwidth matters, but they still quote BPSK as the power-efficiency baseline.
